doc.title: Michael Max Fleming interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

chapter: Rahsaan Roland Kirk and the jazz peak
title: Using his ears, fake books, and the 1945-65 peak of jazz
summary: He refuses to depend on fingers, charts or fake books and says jazz peaked from 1945 to 1965. He later studied reading for studio work.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: No. Never. That’s part of it. Remember what Mary Lou told me, “Don’t you embarrass me.” And so I learned to use my ear, you know, and that was it. On gigs I would go with guys that would play me, “Put the pinkie here.” I wouldn’t give in to that. Even though they were offering that. They’d play a new tune and sometimes I’d act like it but I wouldn’t do that. You know why I wouldn’t do that? This is — I didn’t get this from Mary Lou Williams I just understood that it wasn’t a good thing to do. Because if you get used to watching — because my uncle, in the beginning he would do that sometimes. He would call a tune out, when I went over there with Cleanhead he called out “D minor, G seven, C seven, four beats.” He could do that. He was good. But what I found is if you got accustomed to that there was going to come a time when you’d be in the crook of the piano and you couldn’t see their fingers. Ut um. No. So I can’t do that because that’s going to weaken me. I’m going to develop a dependency. No, no, no, no, no. I don’t do that. Does that make sense to you?
It does indeed. And you know what’s replaced that now is the Internet.

If you want to learn a song it used to be you’d put the record on and you’d play, you’d listen for those bass note. And now you can type it up and there it is for you. And you can start to depend on it.

Yeah well that’s the problem, because I’ve had people that I’ve taught and then I’ve run into them years later. They go on the gig with a little fake book sitting right there. That just turns me off. Maybe it’s okay. But back in the day which as far as I’m concerned from 1945 to 1965, that was when jazz was at its peak. And most of those groups then, if they weren’t big bands, parts of them, Cannonball Adderley, Miles Davis, you never saw

them with music on the bandstand. Think about it. They would be dressed up, and they didn’t do it. So that’s what happened to me. So I came up in that period. And that was all in line with having the ears and everything. And I ran into a shop when I got to the place where I was going to play on Broadway. Because for ten years I hadn’t read any music, although I had gone to a conservatory and studied sight reading and all that stuff. I had formal ear training before I got with Mary Lou, in school. Do-re-me/re-me-fa. Do-re- me/re-me-fa/me-fa-so. I knew all that before I got with her. She didn’t teach me all of that. You know what I’m saying? So yeah, so what I really was trying to do was get into the studios. It was like starting from scratch. Because here I’m doing the other thing, of, “Use your ears,” to like, “play this, play that.” Twelve-eight to four-four. [scats] One- two-three-four-five-six-seven-eight. All kinds of stuff. All kind of crazy rhythms, which we specialized in with Rahsaan. But it wasn’t written out.

Music is wonderful, and it’s limitless. And to me this interview is good because my path is a little different. Everybody’s path is different. Everybody, especially jazz musicians you know. And that was the thing even back in Cincinnati, before I came to New York, do your own thing. That’s what you’re trying — I’m still trying to do it. I still don’t know, what’s my own thing? I’m still, because that’s constantly changing you know. What I did last year might not work this year.
